india-c1e8e5a54a.headline: Slick diplomacy: Trump’s crude u-turn on Russia sanctions bails out India
india-c1e8e5a54a.fulltext:
TOI correspondent from Washington:
 For months, MAGA supremo Donald Trump and his minions threatened to “crush” India’s economy for New Delhi’s purchase of Russian oil. The economics has now caught up with the rhetoric. Faced with soaring fuel prices at home and a widely forecast rout in the mid-term elections, the US President has reversed course and put most of the Russia sanctions on ice, effectively leaving India off the hook for now.
The presidential U-turn, announced in an executive order issued on Friday evening (when governments typically drop bad/embarrassing news), invokes the president’s authority to waive provisions of the Graham Act passed last month “in the national interests of the United States.” Among them: 500% tariffs on Russian goods; 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas (which would include India); and 100% tariffs on the top facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.
The waiver follows Trump's surprise announcement of a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel fuel, even as his administration has turned on Ukraine to end a war that began with Russia's invasion. The deadline to implement the sanctions was to expire on Sunday, one month from the day the bill was passed.
This does not mean sanctions threat has disappeared. The executive order leaves the administration room to reverse course if Trump or designated officials later decide that further action is appropriate. In theory, the president retains leverage; in practice though, a threat that is announced, legislated, signed and then shelved risks becoming less an instrument of coercion than a negotiating prop.
For India, which faced the prospect of tariffs as high as 100 per cent on goods entering the American market under the legislation, the reprieve is welcome -- and well may it send a bill to Washington for economic advice rendered. New Delhi repeatedly insisted that its energy purchases are governed by market conditions, supply security and affordability -- the very argument now being made by Washington. It also maintained steadfastly that its energy decisions cannot simply be dictated by the political preferences of Western capitals.
While the presidential order is admirably concise about the legal manoeuvre, it is considerably less forthcoming about the political embarrassment and diplomatic debacle -- arising mainly from the vituperative hectoring the bill’s authors subjected India to. “If you keep buying cheap Russian oil… we will tariff the hell out of you and we're going to crush your economy,” raged the late Senator Lindsay Graham, who piloted the legislation, warning of tariffs up to 500 per cent. India survived; Graham did not, passing away on July 11 at 71.
Graham’s Democratic co-sponsor Richard Blumenthal was scarcely more restrained. “To China and India: You better clean up your act. Buy your oil and gas somewhere else. Appeasement is not a strategy,” he declared. On Friday, Blumenthal was left fuming at Trump’s appeasement, accusing him of standing “on the side of a bloodthirsty thug and the enablers of Russia’s war machine.”
Forgotten amid the hand-wringing: The Biden administration tacitly encouraged--and explicitly permitted -- India to purchase Russian oil to stabilize global energy supply so long as those purchases adhered to the price cap mechanism. Now, with Graham gone but his legislation very much alive, Trump has discovered that appeasement may not be a strategy either -- but neither is making American motorists pay a premium for geopolitical virtue.
For India, the reprieve is reason enough for a quiet celebration. It was not exactly a Taco Tuesday, but it was certainly a Samosa Saturday in New Delhi: the country Trump threatened to crush for buying cheap Russian oil has been let off the hook by a president who has now discovered the virtues of affordable energy. The oil hasn’t changed, nor has the argument. Only Washington’s position has.

climate-energy-3c1824ba62.headline: China considers new export curbs on solar, AI, biotech
climate-energy-3c1824ba62.fulltext:
China on Friday (October 16, 2026) announced a sweeping draft plan to restrict exports of more than 40 cutting-edge technologies, including solar manufacturing technologies, AI models, and some biotech platforms.
A number of technologies related to the manufacture of solar cells have been listed for either a complete export ban or restricted exports. While the draft plan does not restrict most solar exports, the new controls on next-generation solar manufacturing technologies could impact efforts by countries including India to reduce dependence on China as they look to move up the solar chain.
Several AI-driven technologies have also been listed in the draft plan, announced on Friday by the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology and titled “Announcement No. 48”.
It covers 40 key technologies in the fields of AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics. Of these, 14 technologies were proposed for a complete prohibition of export, including perovskite and tandem solar-cell module manufacturing technologies, AI-driven technology that could be used to generate and mutate malicious code, and some platforms related to cell and gene therapy.
A further 26 technologies were listed for restricted exports, including polysilicon engineering technologies that are used to make solar cells, if they involve production lines with annual output capacities of at least 30,000 tonnes.
Indian manufacturers in the solar space may going forward be impacted including by licensing delays, said Santosh Pai, Honorary Fellow, Institute of Chinese Studies (ICS) and a cross-border lawyer.
“The timetable for localisation is set to launch when domestic capacity from three independent domestic manufacturers exceeds 15 GW. This initial set of domestic manufacturers might experience delays in commencing production due to Announcement 48,” he said. In March, India amended restrictions on Chinese investment imposed in 2020, and listed polysilicon and ingot-wafer segments as priority sectors for fast-track approvals.
These “might not receive traction since Chinese firms will face constraints in undertaking solo investments in India, or joint ventures and licensing deals with Indian counterparts on account of Announcement No. 48,” Mr. Pai noted.
Explaining the move, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a statement that “in recent years, AI, biomedicine and photovoltaic technologies have seen expanding applications in sensitive fields.”
“Major economies around the world have implemented varying degrees of export controls in these areas. Drawing on international practice, China is implementing necessary controls in accordance with the law to prevent risks arising from loss of control over technologies or inappropriate proliferation, while also safeguarding normal international technological cooperation,” the statement said.
On the photovoltaics controls, the statement said China was adding 12 photovoltaic technologies covering polysilicon production, wafer manufacturing and solar-cell manufacturing. Citing the need to “safeguard national security and interests”, the statement said “photovoltaic technologies are increasingly being used in aerospace, defence, unmanned systems and other sensitive sectors; as a result, the national-security implications of technology exports have increased.”
It said “only a limited set of technologies would be regulated” and “other photovoltaic technologies would remain freely exportable.”
On the proposed AI controls, the spokesperson said that while “most AI technologies will continue to be freely exportable”, China was adding 23 key AI technologies covering foundation models, intelligent agents, computing clusters and information-processing technologies.
“Technologies such as autonomous malicious-code generation and mutation could be used to target critical infrastructure, defence systems and core government networks or to evade national security defences,” the statement said. “If such technologies were acquired by malicious actors, they could threaten national security and broader human security. China’s objective is to establish security safeguards, prevent misuse and ensure that AI remains under human control.”
The statement added that China remained “committed to building an open-source AI innovation ecosystem”, and open-source AI projects and overseas chip fabrication activities “would be eligible for facilitation measures” while technologies already in the public domain through open-source publication or academic papers would “generally be exempt from export controls”.

ai-4d4805323d.headline: Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers
ai-4d4805323d.fulltext:
Anthropic, the creator of the AI assistant Claude, confirmed on Friday (October 16, 2026) that it is circulating a draft bill among U.S. lawmakers aimed at regulating artificial intelligence, to address the lack of federal legislation on the risks posed by the technology.
According to the draft, first reported by Politico on Friday (October 16), Washington could block a model’s release or use if there is an imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than $1 billion in damages, but only with a judge’s approval.
A company spokesperson told AFP that the proposal “grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models.” “It requires frontier developers to test the most powerful models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security program,” the spokesperson said.
AI policy in the United States, under President Donald Trump, has relied primarily on voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that tech leaders say is driving the country’s economy. Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after next month’s midterm elections.
Security became a hot topic after recent revelations of security incidents caused by AI agents, autonomous software that operates without constant human supervision, that escaped the control of their developers.
Anthropic, which was banned from the Pentagon by the Trump administration in February 2026, was forced by Washington in June 2026 to suspend its most advanced models for nearly three weeks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry last month to slow down development, fearing that a group of AI agents could take control of “the entire internet” within six to 12 months. Mr. Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as “negative forces.”
The proposed legislation would also override certain State laws, such as those in force in California. Anthropic wrote in June 2026 that “absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate.”
Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think tank praised the proposal as “pretty reasonable,” and “more than other frontier labs have done.” But he said on X that he considered it “weaker” than the FRONTIER Act, a competing bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer.

other-interests-30f643bb5e.headline: Mukesh Ambani's Jio sets price band for India IPO
other-interests-30f643bb5e.fulltext:
[Text below is TechCrunch's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Jio Platforms, the digital arm of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is seeking to raise as much as $3.2 billion in what could be India’s biggest initial public offering. The listing will test public-market appetite for a company that attracted more than $20 billion from global investors, including Google and Meta in 2020.
On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19.
At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering.
In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion (about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion, while Google committed $4.5 billion.
Jio’s IPO is set to overtake Hyundai Motor India’s ₹278.7 billion ($3.3 billion at the time) offering in 2024, the country’s biggest to date, even if its shares are priced at the lower end of the range.
Since launching in 2016, Jio has grown into India’s largest telecom operator, with more than 524 million subscribers as of March 31, ahead of Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It initially drew customers with free data and cheap plans, though its prices are now comparable to those of its rivals. Over time, Jio has grown beyond a telco and expanded into broadband, cloud services, and other digital businesses.
Jio’s IPO comes as Elon Musk has stepped up his criticism of Ambani, accusing him of trying to keep Starlink out of India. The accusation comes more than a year after Jio and rival Airtel signed deals with Musk’s SpaceX to distribute Starlink’s satellite internet service in India, subject to regulatory approvals. Indian authorities have rejected Musk’s claims.
In the quarter ended June, Jio’s revenue rose nearly 12% from a year earlier to ₹391.7 billion (about $4.1 billion), while its net profit climbed 9% to ₹77.6 billion (around $816 million), per its IPO prospectus (PDF).
Jio has set aside shares worth up to ₹25 billion (about $263 million) for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders and another ₹5 billion ($53 million) for employees, who will receive a discount of ₹54 per share.
Of the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion ($2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remaining proceeds going toward general corporate purposes, per the prospectus.

global-economics-24e5932aa3.headline: Who are Deepak Parekh and Paresh Sukthankar? Former HDFC and HDFC Bank execs Prem Watsa is consulting for IDBI Bank deal
global-economics-24e5932aa3.fulltext:
Written By Jocelyn FernandesUpdated17 Oct 2026, 02:00 PM IST
Fairfax Financial Holdings will acquire a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for around ₹53,000 crore ($5.5 billion), in what is poised to become the largest foreign investment in an Indian bank.
Fairfax will engage former HDFC Chairman Deepak Parekh and former HDFC Bank Deputy MD Paresh Sukthankar, as advisors to help it with its proposed acquisition, the Hindu BusinessLine reported on Friday, 16 October.
The deal was approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), and the Canadian company will purchase the government's 30.48% stake (for about ₹26,620 crore) and state-run Life Insurance Corporation of India's (LIC) 30.24% (for about ₹26,440 crore), as per a PTI report.
Billionaire founder Prem Watsa expects that the new combined company will continue to be led by IDBI's current CEO and MD Rakesh Sharma, the HBL report said, adding that Fairfax has sorted out its leadership picks for the lender.
The executive suite will reportedly comprise former CSB Bank CEO CVR Rajendran, and NS Kannan, former MD and CEO of ICICI Prudential Life Company MD and Chief Financial Officer of ICICI Bank. The report added that Kannan is set to take up the role of Chairman, subject to RBI approval.
Notably, the sale process for IDBI Bank began in 2022 and faced a setback earlier this year when initial bids fell below the government's reserve price. The deal is awaiting approval from the central bank, which will conduct a “fit and proper” assessment, and the Competition Commission of India (CCI) and other statutory authorities, the PTI report added.
Chairman of the erstwhile non-banking finance company HDFC, Deepak Parekh stepped down from his position in June 2023 after the merger of HDFC and HDFC Bank. He dubbed the merger as the biggest transaction in India's corporate history and the proposed entity will have combined assets of ₹18 lakh crore.
Parekh joined his uncle’s newly formed Housing Development and Finance Corporation in 1978 as an assistant general manager and turned the mortgage lender into a behemoth. He also spearheaded HDFC’s entry into it with the creation of HDFC Bank.
Over the years, he also held positions as non-independent, non-executive chairman of HDFC Asset Management (a subsidiary of HDFC which runs HDFC Mutual Fund); non-executive chairman of HDFC ERGO General Insurance, HDFC Life Insurance, Glaxo India Ltd, Burroughs Wellcome (India) Ltd, IDFC Ltd and GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals Ltd; and chairman of IDFC Private Equity Co Ltd.
Meanwhile, HDFC Bank’s former Deputy MD Paresh Sukthankar resigned from the lender in August 2018 after a 24-year stint which began in 1994. He was promoted to the post from Executive Director role in March 2017. Analysts and watchers had credited the executive for “taking up the reins after Aditya Puri (then HDFC Bank CEO)”, according to a report by the Financial Express.

indian-startups-7887c6debb.headline: Enterprise AI Startup RapidCanvas Nets $29 Mn To Expand GTM Teams
indian-startups-7887c6debb.fulltext: Enterprise AI startup RapidCanvas has raised $29 Mn (about ₹280 Cr) in its Series B funding round led by Vertex Ventures SEA & India. The round also saw participation from new ventures Hitachi Ventures, along with existing investors Accel, Peak XV Partners, Valley Capital Partners and Titanium Ventures. RapidCanvas will use the proceeds to expand its go-to-market teams and field AI engineering team across India, the US and Brazil. It will also invest in all three products — deepening the Enterprise Context Engine, expanding the skills library behind the Visual Development Canvas, and strengthening governance in the Operational Harness. Founded in 2021 by Rahul Pangam and Uttam Phalnikar, RapidCanvas is an agentic AI startup that helps enterprises build and deploy AI applications as well as oversee their performance. RapidCanvas claims that its annual recurring revenue (ARR) has grown 8X over the past six quarters. So far, in 2026, more than 75 enterprises across manufacturing, financial services, retail, business services and infrastructure have made 1.4 Mn AI-led decisions using applications built on its platform. RapidCanvas follows a subscription-based business model and targets large enterprises that have AI budgets but lack the in-house expertise to move beyond pilot projects. It claims that its platform is "trusted" by companies like PayPal, TresVista, Yale Appliances, Orion, Treetech, among others. "Vibe coding has made it easy to start building with AI. Getting AI into production reliably and safely still remains the biggest gap. Our growth over the past six quarters is evidence that AI in enterprises is moving beyond pilots into production and real operations," said cofounder and CEO Pangam. Enterprise AI Draws Investor Interest RapidCanvas' fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in enterprise tech startups helping businesses deploy AI across their operations. Yesterday, enterprise AI startup Shamrock AI raised $5 Mn in a seed round led by Endiya Partners, with participation from Capria Ventures. A day earlier, Parallel Loop secured $6.6 Mn in a seed round led by 3one4 Capital to help businesses integrate AI into their existing systems and workflows. The trend is also reflected in funding data for the Indian AI ecosystem. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding surged 265% YoY to $438 Mn in the September quarter. Investor sentiment, however, suggests that capital is not flowing indiscriminately across the AI stack. Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half of those who see froth expect a correction within the next 18 months, while another 31% believe valuations are elevated but supported by real revenue. The survey also points to a preference for AI applications that address specific industry needs. Vertical AI applications across sectors such as BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the leading choice, with 39% of investors expecting them to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%.

india-deep-tech-09f84760c4.headline: DRDO Successfully Tests Quantum-Secured Communication System on Live Military Network
india-deep-tech-09f84760c4.fulltext:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has successfully configured and tested a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform on the live network of the dynamic test ranges at the Proof and Experimental Establishment (PXE), Chandipur, Odisha. The development advances India’s capabilities in quantum-secured communications by demonstrating the practical use of QKD to protect real-time critical observations and telemetry generated during artillery and armoured weapon tests and evaluations.
According to the DRDO announcement issued on 14 October 2026, the platform was designed and developed under the organisation’s Microelectronic Devices, Computational Systems and Cyber Security (MCC) cluster in collaboration with production partner Taqbit Labs. It is intended to provide unconditional security for key distribution together with eavesdropping detection.
In its statement, DRDO said: “Advancing India’s capabilities in quantum-secured communications, DRDO successfully configured and tested Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform in the live network of the dynamic test ranges at Proof & Experimental Establishment (PXE), Chandipur. This demonstrates the adept use case of QKD to fortify the real-time critical observations & telemetry associated with Artillery and Armoured Weapon tests and evaluation.” The organisation further noted that the system “will aptly provide unconditional security added with eavesdropping detection.”
Quantum Key Distribution uses the principles of quantum physics—typically the transmission of individual photons—to generate and share cryptographic keys between authorised parties. Any attempt to intercept or measure the quantum signal disturbs its state, enabling immediate detection of eavesdropping.
The resulting keys can then be used with conventional encryption methods to secure data. This approach offers information-theoretic (unconditional) security for the key exchange itself, independent of the computational power available to an adversary, while the overall security of a communication system also depends on proper implementation and protection of connected devices and networks.
The Chandipur trial places the technology in an operational military test-range environment. Weapon trials at PXE generate substantial volumes of sensitive real-time data, including telemetry, sensor readings, performance parameters and technical observations that are transmitted between multiple centres. Securing this information with QKD helps protect it against interception and flags any eavesdropping attempt.
This demonstration follows earlier progress. On 14 July 2026, DRDO and Taqbit Labs completed military field trials of a scalable, practically secure, fibre-based QKD system. That milestone was described as laying the foundation for large-scale, multi-hop quantum networks that are indigenously designed and capable of safeguarding national communication infrastructure against emerging cyber threats in the quantum era.
Taqbit Labs, a Bengaluru-based firm, has been working with DRDO on QKD systems for the Indian Armed Forces since 2020, developing solutions suitable for integration with existing networks as well as new deployments.
PXE at Chandipur is a long-established DRDO laboratory responsible for design and developmental trials of guns, mortars, rockets, tank guns and their ammunition, as well as performance evaluation of tank armour and related systems. Its coastal range supports extensive testing activities, making secure transmission of trial data a relevant operational requirement.
The successful configuration and testing of the QKD platform on a live defence network represents a concrete step in applying indigenous quantum technology to protect sensitive military information during weapons evaluation.
It contributes to broader national efforts to develop quantum-safe communication capabilities for strategic applications. DRDO has not released further technical parameters such as specific link distances, key rates or detailed performance metrics from the Chandipur demonstration.

health-tech-38a375f2ea.fulltext:
[Text below is Al Jazeera's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Kenya confirms four more Ebola cases, bringing total to seven
Three health workers who treated the country’s first Ebola patient are among the latest confirmed cases.
The Kenyan government says four new patients have tested positive for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, bringing the total number of confirmed cases in the East African nation to seven.
Three of the new cases were among health workers who treated the country’s first patient, Kenya’s Ministry of Health said in a statement posted on X on Saturday.
The fourth case is a relative of that same patient, who died from the disease, it added.
The relative had been in quarantine since October 6, the ministry said.
This comes a day after Kenya confirmed three cases in the country. The patient identified on Friday was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, the Health Ministry said.
Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which has recorded more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May.
Kenya’s index patient died on October 5 after being ill in the DRC for a month and then flying to Nairobi on October 3. The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya.
Of the first patient’s 130 contacts, the Health Ministry said 128, or 98.5 percent, had been quarantined – above the global benchmark of 85 percent to break the chain of transmission.
The ministry says it has traced and quarantined nearly all of the first patient’s contacts and there is no evidence that the virus is spreading in the community.
Kenya has reacted quickly by strengthening screening and establishing a hotline for anyone who suspects they may have been in contact with an Ebola patient, but some observers have questioned how the index patient managed to bypass health screenings upon returning to Kenya and make contact with so many people.
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing.
The dominant strain in this outbreak is the Bundibugyo strain, for which there are currently no vaccines or treatments. This has complicated efforts to control the spread of the disease.
Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain, and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans.

DeepSeek pushes out ‘faster, leaner’ updated AI model
DeepSeek released an update of its AI model this weekend that it says is faster and leaner, ramping up the Chinese company’s challenge to Silicon Valley rivals Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as domestic competitors like Moonshot Kimi and Z.ai.
The firm unveiled the V4.1-Flash-1017 in the late afternoon on Oct 17 with a series of posts on X saying the update had “stronger benchmark performance, faster task completion, and shorter outputs than the previous version”.
The model is live across the web, on DeepSeek’s app and its platform for developers.
The rapid pace of DeepSeek’s new launches underscores the intensifying contest between China’s open-weight models and the proprietary models of their US counterparts, which are top performers, but with far higher costs.
DeepSeek’s latest iteration delivers “substantial improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic tasks and visual benchmarks”, the Hangzhou-based start-up said in its technical report on Hugging Face, the online platform for AI models, data sets and apps.
The model released on Oct 17 improves capabilities in uses ranging from game creation to 3D modelling. The company described the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 as a minor update to its earlier V4.1-Flash.
Earlier this week, DeepSeek suffered an outage of about five hours, leaving its servers unreachable. Some experts attributed the glitch to a lack of sufficient computing resources.
Slowdowns and service disruptions have increased in recent months for DeepSeek, whose aggressively priced AI models are sought after by developers, putting pressure on its services.
The Oct 17 model update was preceded by the slimmed down V4.1-Flash AI system, unveiled early in September.
DeepSeek offered it at such a steep discount that shares of rivals such as MiniMax Group, Z.ai and even the giant Alibaba Group Holding, which is driving its Qwen models, plummeted on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
The latest update seeks to be a stronger, faster and more compact version of its predecessor.
DeepSeek disclosed benchmarking scores for its latest update on X. On Humanity’s Last Exam, the revised model scored 36.8 to 42.6, an improvement on V4.1-Flash, which scored 36.8 to 39.1.

Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.
According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)
However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

Isro Successfully Tests Next-gen LME1100 Engine to Power Future Lunar Missions
The Indian space agency successfully conducted the first ignition test of the full-scale gas generator for its 1,100-kN LOX-Methane (LME1100) engine on October 9, marking an important milestone in the next-gen development programme.
Nellore: Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) has made significant progress in developing an indigenous liquid oxygen (LOX)-Methane rocket engine, a key technology for its Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV) and the future human-rated heavy-lift launch vehicle for crewed lunar landing missions targeted in 2040.
The Indian space agency successfully conducted the first ignition test of the full-scale gas generator for its 1,100-kN LOX-Methane (LME1100) engine on October 9, marking an important milestone in the next-gen development programme.
Isro initiated work on LOX-Methane propulsion in 2019, considering its cleaner combustion, lower maintenance requirements and suitability for reusable launch vehicles.
The technology could also support future Mars missions, as methane can potentially be produced using resources available on that planet.
As part of the initial effort, Isro developed and tested a 20-tonne-thrust technology demonstrator engine during 2019–20.
One cold-flow test and five hot tests provided crucial inputs on engine ignition, start-up, combustion, cooling and turbopump performance.
Building on this experience, the agency formally launched the development of the LME1100 in 2023.
Designed around a gas-generator cycle, the engine focuses on cost-effectiveness and ease of industrial production.
More than 70 per cent of its components have been manufactured using additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, with active participation from Indian industries.
The gas generator is undergoing qualification tests at Isro's Propulsion Complex (IPRC).
Sub-scale thrust chamber tests have helped optimise injector configurations and validate ignition systems.
LOX and methane turbopumps, bearings, and dynamic sealing systems are undergoing various stages of testing at the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) and IPRC.
The integrated LME1100 engine is targeted for completion by mid-2027, followed by extensive hot tests to qualify it under different operating conditions, including varying thrust levels.
In the interim, Isro has completed designs of a more powerful 2,400-kN LOX-Methane engine based on the full-flow staged combustion cycle.
The engine is expected to power a future heavy-lift human-rated launch vehicle, strengthening India's capability for crewed lunar exploration.

health-tech-2cd6484e96.headline: How is AI-MedTech in India regulated?
health-tech-2cd6484e96.fulltext:
The national telemedicine consultation helpline e-Sanjeevani has integrated an AI-enabled clinical decision support system for healthcare providers. This is just the latest example of AI’s increasing integration into medicine and medical care worldwide, and in India. As AI begins to influence clinical decisions, such as reassurance, referrals, or investigations, its regulation has now become an urgent patient-safety question. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation’s (CDSCO) July 2026 guidance on software in medical devices becomes important in this context. The document brings software (including AI-enabled) used for a medical purpose into a clearer approval pathway. However, it explicitly says that it reflects existing practice and is not a new regulatory control.
What is MedTech?
Medtech refers to instruments, apparatus, implants, software, or related devices used for diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, or treatment, whose primary action is not achieved through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means. A thermometer, glucometer, blood pressure apparatus, pacemaker, dialysis machine, and CT scanner are considered MedTech. Software is the set of instructions that makes a digital device work. A digital blood-pressure monitor, for example, uses embedded software to control cuff inflation, read pressure sensors and calculate the final BP value. Within software are algorithms, which are step-by-step rules that convert inputs into outputs.
AI (built on advanced algorithms such as machine learning and deep learning models) learns patterns from large amounts of data and uses them to make inferences. All AI depends on algorithms, but not every algorithm is AI. Netflix and YouTube recommendations are familiar examples of algorithms. But a medical algorithm is not a film recommendation. AI may reduce workload, improve consistency and extend specialist support to places where it is scarce. But a false positive can send a healthy person through anxiety and unnecessary tests, while a false negative can do the opposite. A model trained on one population, or one hospital network, may behave differently elsewhere. So, a model that works in Boston is not automatically ready for Bihar.
Risk before labels
India currently regulates medical devices by stretching the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which was intended mainly to penalise spurious drugs. In 1982, an amendment allowed the government to classify devices as ‘drugs’. The Medical Devices Rules, 2017, established the first dedicated rulebook. The rules introduced four classes - Class A for low risk, B for low-to-moderate risk, C for moderate-to-high risk, and D for high risk. The manufacture of devices under classes A and B is generally handled by State licensing authorities, while the central authority regulates manufacture of devices under classes C and D as well as the import of all classes. In 2020, all devices meant for medical use, including software, came under the law. While AI does not create a fifth class, the risk it poses depends on its intended use and the consequences of incorrect output.
The July guidance translates this risk-based approach classification specifically to software as Software in a Medical Device (SiMD - embedded in or controlling hardware), or Software as a Medical Device (SaMD -where the software itself performs the medical function). Software that only stores or transfers patient information is treated differently from one that influences diagnosis or treatment. Standalone medical software is assessed according to both the severity of the clinical situation and the extent to which its output guides medical decisions. Software intended solely for general wellness or routine tracking of body parameters may remain outside the medical-device framework.
Proof followed by surveillance
Validation for AI-enabled devices is sought uniquely. The CDSCO seeks evidence of a sound clinical association between the output and the condition; whether the software technically produces the intended result, and whether it performs clinically in the population and setting (deployment) where it will be used.
Developers are expected to describe training, validation and test datasets, including demographic, geographic and clinical diversity when using AI. Models developed outside India may require justification and validation in representative Indian populations. Bias, generalisability and subgroup performance matter because even ‘95% accurate’ means little without asking — accurate at what, in whom, and against which reference standard? Approval is also a continuous process as algorithms can be retrained, software can be upgraded, while performance can drift. The CDSCO discusses change in management, retraining, rollback, version control and post-market surveillance of the system.
Guidelines, not law
India’s AI regulation is outlined in policy papers of NITI Aayog, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. In 2018, NITI Aayog released the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, which named health care a priority. ICMR then, in 2023, issued ethical guidelines for AI in health care, stressing the need for accountability, fairness and patient autonomy. In November 2025, the Electronics & IT Ministry’s AI Governance Guidelines chose not to propose a separate AI law, leaving each sector’s regulator to act.
In February 2026, the Health Ministry launched the Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare for India (SAHI), which addresses governance, data, validation, deployment and monitoring of AI across healthcare. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has developed AI-specific lifecycle approaches, including predetermined change-control plans for defined future modifications. Europe combines medical-device regulation with the EU AI Act, which adds requirements for high-risk AI such as risk management, data quality and human oversight.
Way forward
The new guidance raises a larger question: can a technology that decides who is sick and who is sent home be governed by guidelines alone? India’s guideline-led approach has enabled regulators to move quickly without waiting for Parliamentary legislation. While its insistence on Indian data is ahead of many similar guidelines elsewhere, a dedicated statute for AI-enabled medical devices could make Indian validation mandatory for high-risk tools, clarify liability, and create a public registry of approved AI devices.
The question is whether technologies that can influence life-and-death decisions should continue to rely on guidance built on an 80-year-old law or be governed by a clear statutory framework that patients and clinicians can trust.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

agritech-9b2be1a39b.headline: India restricts sugarcane-based ethanol procurement as poor monsoon tightens sugar supplies
agritech-9b2be1a39b.fulltext:
India has stopped state-run oil companies from buying ethanol made from sugar and key sugarcane-based materials for the next supply year, a move that could help preserve sugar supplies as poor rainfall threatens domestic production.
The restriction will take effect from November 1, when the new ethanol supply year begins.
The decision comes after a weak monsoon and El Nino-related dry weather hurt sugarcane output, tightening supplies and pushing up global sugar prices.
India is the world's second-largest sugar producer, and a smaller crop has raised concerns about the availability of the sweetener.
According to a report by Bloomberg, five state-owned fuel companies have issued a joint tender for nearly 11 billion litres of ethanol for the coming supply year, following the government's directions.
The tender excludes ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses.
The move could help keep more sugarcane-derived material available for sugar production at a time when supplies are under pressure.
However, the restrictions do not amount to a complete halt to ethanol procurement, as oil companies can still source the fuel from other permitted raw materials.
The tender was issued by Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation, Numaligarh Refinery and Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals, the report said.
It allows suppliers to offer ethanol made from C-heavy molasses, damaged food grains, surplus rice held by the Food Corporation of India, corn and other feedstocks permitted under the National Policy on Biofuels.
India has expanded ethanol production over the past few years to reduce its dependence on imported crude oil and provide sugarcane farmers with an additional source of income.
Sugar mills have also benefited from selling ethanol to oil companies instead of relying entirely on sugar sales.
The government had advanced its target of blending 20 per cent ethanol into petrol by five years, and India achieved the goal in 2025.
The latest restrictions could limit the use of sugarcane-based feedstocks for ethanol during the next supply year.
At the same time, allowing procurement from corn, damaged grains and other approved sources gives oil companies alternative ways to meet their blending requirements.

agritech-d20b6e0e9a.headline: Maharashtra's monsoon deficit raises concern as El Niño threatens warmer winter, rabi crops
agritech-d20b6e0e9a.fulltext:
MUMBAI: Maharashtra's deficient monsoon, coupled with a developing potentially strong El Niño, has raised concerns over water security, rabi crop stress and food prices. Meteorologists have warned that a warmer-than-normal winter could bring summer-like conditions as early as February 2027.
The state received 804.4mm of rainfall during the June-September monsoon, against the normal of 994.5mm, a shortfall of about 19%. Nineteen of its 36 districts recorded deficient rainfall. Marathwada was the worst-hit subdivision, with a 39% deficit, followed by Vidarbha at 27%. The Konkan region fared relatively better, with only one of its seven districts recording deficient rainfall.
The impact could extend into the next crop cycle, as depleted soil moisture, lower groundwater recharge and stressed reservoirs increase irrigation requirements. For Mumbai and the metropolitan region, water availability will depend on reservoir storage, subsequent inflows and demand.
A Climate Trends analysis dated October 16 says Maharashtra is among five states, along with Telangana, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan, that have declared drought. Its claim that drought affects 75% of Maharashtra needs to be verified against the relevant government notification.
Reservoirs, crops under pressure
Central Water Commission data cited in the report show that live storage in 178 monitored reservoirs stood at 78.71% of the corresponding period last year and 87.08% of normal as of October 8. The western region's storage stood at 82.42% of its normal level.
Nationally, rice acreage as of October 5 was down by 15.56 lakh hectares compared with the corresponding period in 2025-26, including a decline of 1.15 lakh hectares in Maharashtra. Sugarcane and cotton acreage also fell, while the area under pulses and oilseeds increased, potentially reflecting a shift towards less water-intensive crops. However, changes in acreage do not necessarily indicate final production losses.
Dr G V Ramanjaneyulu, executive director of the Centre for Sustainable Agriculture, said prolonged dry spells reduce soil moisture and groundwater recharge, increasing dependence on irrigation. He advocated the cultivation of short-duration pulses, oilseeds and millets, along with better soil management.
Rainfall deficits across the country
India's monsoon ended with a 13% rainfall deficit, its weakest performance in a decade, according to the analysis. East and Northeast India received 1,017.1mm of rainfall against the normal of 1,367.3mm, a shortfall of 25.6% and the region's lowest monsoon total since 1901. The South Peninsula recorded 542mm against the normal of 716mm, its fourth-lowest monsoon total since 1901.
Bihar recorded deficient rainfall in 33 of its 38 districts, Assam in 22 of 35, Arunachal Pradesh in 12 of 16, and Meghalaya in 10 of 11. Karnataka recorded a statewide deficit of 30%, Kerala 28%, Andhra Pradesh 25% and Tamil Nadu 20%. Ramanagara in Karnataka recorded a 91% shortfall, while Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu recorded a deficit of 64%. Central and northwest India received near-normal rainfall.
Warmer winter, tougher rabi season
The report cites an 83% probability of El Niño becoming the strongest event since 1950 during October-December, with conditions highly likely to persist until February 2027. The India Meteorological Department forecast cited in the analysis points to below-normal winter rainfall across most of India and above-average temperatures. However, these remain projections rather than certainties.
The reported foodgrain production target for 2026-27 is 373.93 million tonnes, 2.63 million tonnes below the estimated output for 2025-26. Dr K J Ramesh, former director-general of the India Meteorological Department, warned that low groundwater levels and reduced soil moisture could affect rabi and summer crops. Climate scientist Dr Roxy Mathew Koll said global warming raises background temperatures and can intensify the impacts of El Niño.
Aarti Khosla, director of Climate Trends, called for stronger early-warning systems, heat-action plans and public-health preparedness.
For Maharashtra, the priorities are to safeguard drinking-water supplies, monitor reservoir levels, support farmers in selecting crops suited to available soil moisture and prepare for heat. The end of the monsoon may mark the beginning, rather than the end, of a prolonged period of climate stress.

indian-startups-769d0e73d3.headline: Decoding Urban Company’s ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise Proposal
indian-startups-769d0e73d3.fulltext: Listed home services major Urban Company’s board approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr yesterday, seeking to shore up its war chest at a critical juncture. On one hand, Urban Company’s instant home services business, InstaHelp, is facing stiff competition. Fighting rivals Snabbit and Pronto for a slice of the market has turned out to be an expensive affair, with spending on InstaHelp contributing to Urban Company’s widening losses. At the same time, the company is looking to expand its product lineup under the Native brand by entering the residential air conditioner market. Meanwhile, its bread and butter consumer services continue to generate stable results. Urban Company’s financials reflect these pressures. The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by a ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding InstaHelp, it reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹30 Cr. During the quarter, consolidated revenue from operations grew 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr, while total expenses increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr. Consequently, the company’s consolidated net loss more than tripled to ₹182.5 Cr from ₹59.3 Cr in the year-ago period. However, the management maintains that Urban Company can meet its profitability targets without the proposed fundraise Yet, the management has rejected the suggestion that the fundraise is necessary to offset InstaHelp’s impact on its financials. How Badly Does Urban Company Need The Cash? Urban Company has positioned the proposed ₹2,500 Cr fundraise as a means to bolster its balance sheet and provide greater flexibility to invest across its businesses. “Our ambition is to go beyond being just a home services company and eventually become the trusted home platform for Indian consumers – almost the operating system for the Indian home. So given that ambition, we want the strategic flexibility over the next few years to invest in all our areas of business,” CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal told analysts during the company’s Q2 FY27 earnings call. The company also plans to deploy the capital towards growth opportunities, including acquisitions. While no acquisition deals have been finalised till now, the management is evaluating opportunities that could help Urban Company consolidate its position in an existing market or enter a new category. Bhal added that the company would take an opportunistic approach to international markets and Native. However, an acquisition in InstaHelp would be “highly unlikely”. “If at all we do an M&A, it would be to add on categories that we don’t operate in today where we feel that the decision of build versus buy may be tilting in favour of buy,” he noted. Urban Company has guided for adjusted EBITDA breakeven by Q3 FY28 and ₹1,000 Cr in adjusted EBITDA profit by FY31. The management maintained that its current financial position, even without raising additional capital, is sufficient to meet these targets. However, Bhal acknowledged that the company’s existing balance sheet limits its financial flexibility, given InstaHelp’s losses. While the management maintains that the company can meet its profitability targets without additional capital, the proposed fundraise would provide it with greater room to invest in growth and respond to changing market conditions. In particular, Urban Company is facing intense competition in the emerging quick home services segment. For instance, after Urban Company disclosed that InstaHelp completed 6.2 Mn orders in Q2, Snabbit's founder Aayush Agarwal claimed that the startup had served 6.45 Mn orders during the period. Diving Into A New Market While it faces intense competition in the quick home services market, Urban Company is simultaneously looking to expand into a new category. Alongside approving the fundraise proposal, its board proposed exploring residential air conditioners as a new business under its consumer appliances brand Native, whose portfolio currently comprises water purifiers and smart locks. “We’ve now operated in the segment of air conditioning servicing and repair for close to 11-12 years, ever since the inception of the company. And there’s a lot of data and knowledge that we have gathered on what are the consumer pain points and what are some of the unmet needs of the consumers. Based on those data points and our own understanding of the market and the unmet needs, we have been quietly working on creating an innovative cutting-edge product,” Bhal told analysts on the call. The company is yet to disclose further details, including a commercial launch timeline. Notably, Inc42 reported last year about Urban Company’s potential foray into AC business. Bhal said the first one to two years in the new market would focus on learning and gathering customer feedback. He also noted that Urban Company’s app would be the sole distribution channel for its ACs. The CEO emphasised a “calibrated and measured” approach to capital allocation, adding that Native has a clear path to profitability that should not be affected by the new venture. For context, Native’s net transaction value (NTV) grew 35.4% YoY in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue rose 40% to ₹105 Cr. The segment remained loss-making on an adjusted EBITDA basis, reporting a loss of ₹9 Cr. However, loss as a percentage of NTV declined to 6.8% from 9% a year ago. Urban Company’s platform sees 10X as many AC servicing, repair, and installation orders as water purifier orders, giving it a larger existing customer base for AC-related services. This provides a potential channel to market Native’s ACs, although service demand does not necessarily translate into appliance sales. With InstaHelp facing stiff competition and Native preparing to enter a new product category, Urban Company is pursuing multiple growth opportunities even as its losses widen. The proposed fundraise would provide additional capital to support these plans, although the management maintains that the company can achieve its stated profitability targets without it.

indian-startups-e5bbcae9ec.headline: Cult.fit gets SEBI nod for proposed IPO
indian-startups-e5bbcae9ec.fulltext:
Fitness and lifestyle platform Cult.fit has received observations from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its proposed initial public offering (IPO).
The company, formerly known as Curefit Healthcare, plans to raise Rs 950 crore through a fresh issue of equity shares, alongside an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 17.86 crore shares by existing shareholders.
The proceeds from the fresh issue will be used to repay borrowings, set up new Cult Elite and Cult Neo fitness centres, expand Cultsport’s exclusive brand outlets, meet lease and rental payments for existing centres, and fund brand marketing and general corporate purposes.
According to the company’s draft papers, Cult.fit operates 708 fitness centres across 77 cities in India as of March 31, 2026. Its fitness services business had nearly 9.87 lakh paid members in FY26, while its fitness products business shipped over 42.3 lakh products during the year.
The company operates across two key segments, fitness services and fitness products. Fitness services contributed around 70% of its revenue, while fitness products accounted for the remaining 30%.
Cult.fit’s operating revenue rose 36.26% year-on-year to Rs 1,720.61 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 1,262.93 crore in FY25. The company had reported operating revenue of Rs 926.66 crore in FY24.
Its adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 8.41% in FY26 from -2.76% in FY25, according to the draft papers.
The company operates different formats of fitness centres, including Cult Elite, which combines gym workouts with instructor-led group classes, and Cult Neo, a gym format focused on equipment-based workouts. Its fitness products business sells apparel, footwear, equipment and accessories under the Cultsport brand.
Cult.fit has also built a technology-led platform that connects its fitness services and products businesses through its app, website and offline channels.
The proposed IPO comes amid growth in India’s organised fitness market. According to the Redseer report cited in the draft papers, the country’s fitness services market was estimated at Rs 25,600 crore in CY25 and is projected to reach Rs 48,700 crore to Rs 53,100 crore by CY30.
The equity shares will be listed on the BSE and NSE.
Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs India Securities, Jefferies India, JM Financial and Morgan Stanley India are the book-running lead managers to the issue.

indian-startups-7c3d0f8997.headline: Snabbit FY26 loss widens multifold to Rs 167.75 Cr; revenue rises to Rs 12.25 Cr
indian-startups-7c3d0f8997.fulltext:
Its revenue from operations rose to Rs 12.25 crore in FY26 from Rs 26.35 lakh a year earlier. Platform services brought in Rs 10.82 crore, and the sale of uniforms to its service providers, whom it calls experts, stood at Rs 1.42 crore.
Maestroedge Solutions, which runs home services platform Snabbit, has posted a net loss of Rs 167.75 crore for 2025-26, nearly 30 times lower than the previous year, as spending on service providers, marketing and staff rose with the expansion of its business, according to financial statements filed with the Registrar of Companies.
The Mumbai-based company reported a loss of Rs 5.70 crore in FY25.
Its revenue from operations rose to Rs 12.25 crore in FY26 from Rs 26.35 lakh a year earlier.
Platform services brought in Rs 10.82 crore, and the sale of uniforms to its service providers, whom it calls experts, stood at Rs 1.42 crore.
Other income was Rs 14.77 crore, while total income was recorded at Rs 27 crore.
Total expenses rose to Rs 194.76 crore from Rs 6.81 crore in FY25. Expert service cost was the largest expense at Rs 63.07 crore, up from Rs 27 lakh. Marketing spending rose nearly 60-fold to Rs 48.69 crore. Employee benefit expenses grew to Rs 46.02 crore from Rs 3.27 crore, and service fulfilment expenses to Rs 23.83 crore from Rs 48 lakh.
"FY26 was our first full year of operations, and we made a deliberate choice to invest ahead of scale to build a category, not just a company," Snabbit founder and CEO Aayush Agarwal said.
Agarwal said the company began the year with about 500 jobs a day across eight micro-markets and ended it at a run rate of 35,000 daily jobs across more than 100 micro-markets. During the year, it acquired nearly a million customers and onboarded over 20,000 experts, according to Agarwal.
Losses were mainly due to investments in geographic expansion, customer and expert acquisition, and long-term operating capabilities, Agarwal added.
The company was incorporated in January 2024. Its platform lets customers book house help, with an initial focus on maids for cleaning and cooking.
The company had 309 employees as of March 31, 2026. Agarwal, who holds 98.98% of its equity shares, drew a salary of Rs 60 lakh in FY26, up from Rs 15.47 lakh.
"Given the pace of growth and the investments required to build this category from the ground up, FY26 financials do not fully reflect the underlying economics or the maturity of the business today.
"As we continue to scale, the benefits of operating leverage, improving unit economics and increasing network density are becoming increasingly evident," Agarwal said.

india-deep-tech-bdee98e295.headline: Space robotics startup Cosmochute raises $1.5 Mn in pre-seed round
india-deep-tech-bdee98e295.fulltext:
Space robotics startup Cosmochute has raised $1.5 million in a pre-seed funding round led by Accel and Prosus Ventures under the Atoms X programme. IIMA Ventures’ Deep-tech and Aerospace Acceleration Fund, Operators Studio and Chinmayi Muthyala also participated in the round.
Cosmochute is among seven startups selected for the inaugural Atoms X cohort, which was launched earlier this year.
The company will use the proceeds for product development, engineering team expansion and its commercial roadmap, as it prepares for its next phase of growth, Cosmochute said in a press release.
Founded this year by Janhavi Gore, Amit Chowdhary and Dhruv Alok Sangal, Cosmochute is building space robotics infrastructure for the emerging lunar economy. Its first programme, LEAP, is a modular platform designed to support payload transportation and deployment on the Moon.
LEAP combines a modular rover and trailer with standard payload bays, allowing multiple payloads to be integrated into a common mission architecture. The company aims to address the cost and complexity of delivering equipment and payloads to the lunar surface through a standardised approach to lunar transportation and deployment.
The platform is designed to reduce the need for mission specific engineering and make lunar transportation and payload deployment more repeatable.
Cosmochute is setting up its lunar laboratories at IIMA Ventures’ incubation facility. The startup is also working within India’s space technology ecosystem, which includes companies, investors and institutions supporting private participation in the sector.
With LEAP as its first platform, Cosmochute plans to develop capabilities in lunar mobility and space robotics, with potential applications in other in space and terrestrial use cases. The company aims to build infrastructure to support commercial and scientific missions to the Moon.

india-deep-tech-7f1d196dd3.headline: DRDO develops portable system to sniff out enemy radars, track drone threats
india-deep-tech-7f1d196dd3.fulltext:
The 
Defence Research and Development Organisation
 (
DRDO
) is moving to develop man-portable electronic intelligence modules, a compact system meant to pick up and analyse the signals that enemy radars or any other antennas emit. The tender has been issued by the Defence Electronics Research Laboratory (DRDL) located in Hyderabad. Electronic intelligence, or ELINT, is the practice of capturing signals from radars and other electronic equipment and studying them to work out what kind of system is operating and its technical characteristics are. A radar or an drone operator could be emitting signals, which could inform about the frequency range of the device sending out signals. This could help jam the system more effectively, focussing on those particular frequencies and thereby rendering the effectiveness of the system.
The process begins with the antenna and receiver, which pick up signals across several frequency bands, since different radars work on different frequencies. The system then measures the signal's characteristics, including frequency, pulse width, the interval between pulses, the number of pulses sent in a given time, signal strength, direction of arrival and the modulation within the signal.
In an operational area, several radars may be active at once and their signals reach the receiver together. 
Separating them is known as deinterleaving, and it relies on frequency, timing between pulses and other inbuilt features, with digital processing and machine learning used in modern systems. The separated signal is then compared with a library of known radar signatures, which lets the system judge what type of radar is being used to, be it a search radar, a tracking radar or a fire control radar. Search radars scan a wide area for targets, tracking radars keep watch on a particular target and fire control radars support the use of weapons.
Portability for such a system is important, especially in mountainous and remote terrain, where deploying large vehicles or fixed surveillance equipment could be difficult. A small system can give field formations information on electronic activity without depending on assets available with larger platforms. In an era, where drones are taking centre stage, the deployment of such systems could help pinpoint the location of a drone operator or could give early waring of an approaching inimical drone, thus providing own forces more time to activate counter drone drills.
The system can also estimate where a signal is coming from. If sensors at different locations pick up the same signal, their readings can be combined to estimate a location, using techniques such as triangulation and time difference of arrival of radar waves. Different digital techniques, helps analyse a signal by frequency. Once the signal is identified, the system assesses the threat and a change in a radar's signal may indicate that its mode of operation has changed.
The DRDL project has three separate parts which are defined as development, integration and qualification. Development will cover the equipment and its modules, integration brings the parts together into one working system and qualification tests it against technical and environmental standards, including temperature, humidity, vibration, shock and electromagnetic interference.

global-economics-3a9f1a542e.headline: Anthropic offers Blackstone double-digit yield in chip-financing deal, FT reports

Written By Sanchari GhoshPublished17 Oct 2026, 08:49 AM IST
Anthropic is offering Blackstone a yield of more than 10% to finance a $60 billion artificial intelligence (AI) chip deal, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The deal is touted to be the largest chip-financing arrangement to date.
Known as Project North Star, the financing will support Anthropic’s acquisition of approximately 1.5 gigawatts of Google’s custom tensor processing units (TPUs), as AI developers race to secure computing capacity.
Blackstone-managed funds are expected to invest $9 billion in junior debt backed by Anthropic’s five-year chip lease payments. This represents half of the planned $18 billion junior financing.
The investment firm has been offered a 10% coupon, with total returns exceeding that level after accounting for issuance discounts and fees. By comparison, similarly rated borrowers typically pay yields of around 7% in public bond markets. The remaining $9 billion in junior debt is expected to be offered to other investors in the coming months, potentially at lower yields.
The financing package also includes approximately $42 billion in senior debt guaranteed by Broadcom, which collaborates with Google on chip development.
The deal follows Anthropic’s Project Big Sky financing, through which the company raised around $4.4 billion at an 8.5% interest rate four months ago. The higher borrowing cost in the latest arrangement reflects growing investor demands for compensation amid concerns over rising AI infrastructure spending.
Anthropic received a credit rating one notch below investment grade from KBRA in June, and the new junior debt is expected to receive a similar assessment. The company is seeking investment-grade status to lower future borrowing costs.
The debt could become tradable in the institutional 144A bond market after the financing is drawn down in 2027.
Earlier this week, Anthropic opened a line of communication with New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, following his letter calling for the artificial intelligence lab to delay its initial public offering.
“It does appear they are under pressure from multiple sides right now,” Levine said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Friday. He couldn’t characterise the discussions with Anthropic, he said.
Levine’s letter dated Wednesday, addressed to Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, urged the company to pause the listing process until it fully and transparently addresses the AI safety and governance concerns it has raised. It said last month’s morally binding safety accord with the Trump administration and AI companies, including Anthropic, was insufficient to meet the moment.
“If they go public and then there is a catastrophic safety incident, beyond, far beyond what we’ve seen right now, that would be terrible for their stock,” Levine said in the interview.
“Much better to take a little more time right now and get this done,” Levine said.
The comptroller looks after the city’s fiscal health and oversees public pension funds with more than $325 billion in assets. Some of those funds are invested in index-tracking funds, according to Levine, who said they assume “the indexes will rush Anthropic in.”

NEW DELHI: Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) on Wednesday said it has successfully configured and tested a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) platform in the live network of the dynamic test ranges at Proof and Experimental Establishment (PXE), Chandipur, thereby advancing India’s capabilities in quantum-secured communications.QKD is a secure communication method that uses the laws of quantum mechanics to let two parties generate a shared and secret random key known only to them, which then can be used to encrypt and decrypt messages.According to DRDO, this demonstrates the adept use case of QKD to fortify the real-time critical observations and telemetry associated with artillery and armoured weapon tests and evaluation. Kenya confirms four more Ebola cases, bringing total to seven
Three health workers who treated the country’s first Ebola patient are among the latest confirmed cases.
The Kenyan government says four new patients have tested positive for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, bringing the total number of confirmed cases in the East African nation to seven.
Three of the new cases were among health workers who treated the country’s first patient, Kenya’s Ministry of Health said in a statement posted on X on Saturday.
The fourth case is a relative of that same patient, who died from the disease, it added.
The relative had been in quarantine since October 6, the ministry said.
This comes a day after Kenya confirmed three cases in the country. The patient identified on Friday was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, the Health Ministry said.
Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which has recorded more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May.
Kenya’s index patient died on October 5 after being ill in the DRC for a month and then flying to Nairobi on October 3. The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya.
Of the first patient’s 130 contacts, the Health Ministry said 128, or 98.5 percent, had been quarantined – above the global benchmark of 85 percent to break the chain of transmission.
The ministry says it has traced and quarantined nearly all of the first patient’s contacts and there is no evidence that the virus is spreading in the community.
Kenya has reacted quickly by strengthening screening and establishing a hotline for anyone who suspects they may have been in contact with an Ebola patient, but some observers have questioned how the index patient managed to bypass health screenings upon returning to Kenya and make contact with so many people.
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing.
The dominant strain in this outbreak is the Bundibugyo strain, for which there are currently no vaccines or treatments. This has complicated efforts to control the spread of the disease.
Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain, and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans.

climate-energy-3ceba0f24d.headline: Why Renault is betting on hybrids in EV 'outlier' India
climate-energy-3ceba0f24d.fulltext:
Why Renault is betting on hybrids in EV 'outlier' India
NEW DELHI, Oct. 17 -- When Stephane Deblaise took charge of Renault's India operations a little over a year ago, he brought a lesson from South Korea: car buyers do not necessarily replace their petrol or diesel cars with electric vehicles (EVs).
His first year in India has reinforced that view. Buyers still weigh engine performance, fuel efficiency, technology and price before choosing a car, the 54-year-old French chief executive told Mint. "The big picture I understood very quickly," he said. "Engines are very important. Value is very important."
That conviction is now shaping Renault's biggest powertrain bet yet on the Indian market: a strong hybrid version of its flagship sport utility vehicle (SUV), the Duster, launched on Saturday.
India's electrification story has so far been led by battery EVs, with strong hybrids lagging behind. EV penetration in passenger vehicles rose to about 8.5% in September from 5.7% a year earlier, according to Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (Fada) data. Strong hybrids, by contrast, have remained at around 2%.
EVs accounted for one-fifth of incremental growth in the car market in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), with electric car sales surging 84% to nearly 200,000 units. Strong hybrids, offered in India by Japanese carmakers Maruti Suzuki, Toyota Kirloskar and Honda Cars, remain a much smaller segment.
But the global experience suggests that the transition away from conventional engines need not be an all-electric one.
In the US, hybrids accounted for 16% of the market in the second quarter of 2026, against 6% for EVs, according to the US Energy Information Administration. In the European Union, hybrids made up 36.6% of new car registrations in the first eight months of 2026, compared with a 21.7% share for battery EVs, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association.
"Even the most advanced country for BEV is not only BEV," Deblaise said.
He argues that the pace of adoption depends as much on policy and customer preferences as on technology. "The percentages are only depending on policies. They are depending on policies and customer appetite."
"The BEV is relatively high these days. It's a huge gap. But it is helped by the 5% tax. If we would not have 5%, it would be 0.5%," he said.
India charges 5% goods and services tax (GST) on EVs, while hybrids have not received equivalent treatment, with these vehicles-mostly large SUVs-taxed at 40%.
For Deblaise, the bigger question is whether customers can adopt electric mobility without compromising on convenience. Charging infrastructure and the time needed to recharge remain constraints, he said. "A car, it is freedom. But a BEV car, today, it is not freedom."
Hybrids offer a way to improve fuel economy without requiring buyers to change how they use their cars. That is the opportunity Renault hopes to exploit with the Duster Strong Hybrid, its first full-hybrid offering in India.
The SUV's 1.8-litre powertrain and 1.4-kWh battery deliver a claimed mileage of 29 km per litre, allowing Renault to pitch it against diesel SUVs that have traditionally attracted buyers seeking fuel efficiency.
"29 kilometres per litre in hybrid is a game changer in India. There is no doubt. Our strong tech hybrid is the new diesel," Deblaise said.
The proposition, however, comes with a price trade-off. Hybrid powertrains cost more than conventional petrol and diesel systems, making the upfront purchase price a key hurdle in a market where value remains central to buying decisions. Renault is banking on localization to improve the economics over time.
Deblaise said the company had spent nearly a decade developing the technology, including its battery and gearbox. "We are not trying to introduce innovation in India to check if our idea is good. We have already done it," he said.
Deblaise's confidence in hybrids draws partly on an earlier decision in South Korea, where engineering constraints prevented Renault from launching hybrid and internal-combustion engine (ICE) versions of a new car simultaneously.
He chose to launch the hybrid first. "I said, okay, we launch first the hybrid," he recalled.
The hybrid eventually accounted for 92% of the car's volumes over its lifecycle, despite a relatively high price gap between the two versions. Deblaise said the result did not mean customers had rejected conventional engines.
"There was nothing against ICE. But we had a very good solution on hybrid," he said.
He does not expect India to replicate South Korea's 92% share. But he believes hybrids can account for a meaningful portion of Renault's sales. "We should have a big part of our volumes. A big two-digit percentage of our volumes in hybrid," he said.
The bet comes as Renault seeks to revive its fortunes in India. According to Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (Siam) data, Renault's sales rose 32% to 23,122 units in April-September 2026, when the Duster rolled out.
