global-economics-51aa7f403a.headline: Why Renault is betting on hybrids in EV ‘outlier’ India
global-economics-51aa7f403a.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: When Stephane Deblaise took charge of Renault’s India operations a little over a year ago, he brought a lesson from South Korea: car buyers do not necessarily replace their petrol or diesel cars with electric vehicles (EVs).
His first year in India has reinforced that view. Buyers still weigh engine performance, fuel efficiency, technology and price before choosing a car, the 54-year-old French chief executive told Mint. “The big picture I understood very quickly,” he said. “Engines are very important. Value is very important.”
That conviction is now shaping Renault’s biggest powertrain bet yet on the Indian market: a strong hybrid version of its flagship sport utility vehicle (SUV), the Duster, launched on Saturday.
India’s electrification story has so far been led by battery EVs, with strong hybrids lagging behind. EV penetration in passenger vehicles rose to about 8.5% in September from 5.7% a year earlier, according to Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (Fada) data. Strong hybrids, by contrast, have remained at around 2%.
EVs accounted for one-fifth of incremental growth in the car market in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), with electric car sales surging 84% to nearly 200,000 units. Strong hybrids, offered in India by Japanese carmakers Maruti Suzuki, Toyota Kirloskar and Honda Cars, remain a much smaller segment.
But the global experience suggests that the transition away from conventional engines need not be an all-electric one.
In the US, hybrids accounted for 16% of the market in the second quarter of 2026, against 6% for EVs, according to the US Energy Information Administration. In the European Union, hybrids made up 36.6% of new car registrations in the first eight months of 2026, compared with a 21.7% share for battery EVs, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association.
“Even the most advanced country for BEV is not only BEV,” Deblaise said.
He argues that the pace of adoption depends as much on policy and customer preferences as on technology. “The percentages are only depending on policies. They are depending on policies and customer appetite.”
“The BEV is relatively high these days. It's a huge gap. But it is helped by the 5% tax. If we would not have 5%, it would be 0.5%,” he said.
India charges 5% goods and services tax (GST) on EVs, while hybrids have not received equivalent treatment, with these vehicles—mostly large SUVs—taxed at 40%.
Mileage versus price
For Deblaise, the bigger question is whether customers can adopt electric mobility without compromising on convenience. Charging infrastructure and the time needed to recharge remain constraints, he said. “A car, it is freedom. But a BEV car, today, it is not freedom.”
Hybrids offer a way to improve fuel economy without requiring buyers to change how they use their cars. That is the opportunity Renault hopes to exploit with the Duster Strong Hybrid, its first full-hybrid offering in India.
The SUV's 1.8-litre powertrain and 1.4-kWh battery deliver a claimed mileage of 29 km per litre, allowing Renault to pitch it against diesel SUVs that have traditionally attracted buyers seeking fuel efficiency.
“29 kilometres per litre in hybrid is a game changer in India. There is no doubt. Our strong tech hybrid is the new diesel,” Deblaise said.
The proposition, however, comes with a price trade-off. Hybrid powertrains cost more than conventional petrol and diesel systems, making the upfront purchase price a key hurdle in a market where value remains central to buying decisions. Renault is banking on localization to improve the economics over time.
Deblaise said the company had spent nearly a decade developing the technology, including its battery and gearbox. “We are not trying to introduce innovation in India to check if our idea is good. We have already done it,” he said.
Lesson from South Korea
Deblaise’s confidence in hybrids draws partly on an earlier decision in South Korea, where engineering constraints prevented Renault from launching hybrid and internal-combustion engine (ICE) versions of a new car simultaneously.
He chose to launch the hybrid first. “I said, okay, we launch first the hybrid,” he recalled.
The hybrid eventually accounted for 92% of the car’s volumes over its lifecycle, despite a relatively high price gap between the two versions. Deblaise said the result did not mean customers had rejected conventional engines.
“There was nothing against ICE. But we had a very good solution on hybrid,” he said.
He does not expect India to replicate South Korea’s 92% share. But he believes hybrids can account for a meaningful portion of Renault’s sales. “We should have a big part of our volumes. A big two-digit percentage of our volumes in hybrid,” he said.
The bet comes as Renault seeks to revive its fortunes in India. According to Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (Siam) data, Renault’s sales rose 32% to 23,122 units in April-September 2026, when the Duster rolled out.
Whether the hybrid strategy can sustain that recovery remains an open question. Deblaise acknowledged that offering customers more choice may not be enough to bring every former or potential buyer back to the brand.
“Some people maybe will never come in Renault because they don't want. It will take time for them to come.”

global-economics-6e97c65ea0.headline: Meet Aayush Agarwal: Snabbit boss explains why ‘house help’ firm suffered ₹168 cr loss on ₹12 cr revenue in FY26
global-economics-6e97c65ea0.fulltext:
Eshita GainPublished17 Oct 2026, 09:22 PM IST Snabbit’s losses widened nearly 30-fold to ₹167.75 crore in fiscal year 2026 (FY26) from ₹5.70 crore in FY25, as the instant house-help startup ramped up spending on workers and marketing to expand its business. Revenue from operations rose to ₹12.25 crore in the year ended 31 March 2026 from ₹26.35 lakh a year earlier, according to financial statements of Maestroedge Solutions Pvt. Ltd, which operates Snabbit. Speaking on LinkedIn about the losses, the startup's founder and chief executive Aayush Agarwal said that building a business from “scratch” requires significant investment, even when spending far exceeds revenue. He said the company “deliberately” invested in customer adoption, workforce training, technology, infrastructure and geographic expansion, adding that it would make the same investments again. “But what an annual P&L doesn't tell you is that at the beginning of FY26, we were losing approximately ₹1,500 per job. Last month, that number was below ₹200. And it continues to improve,” he noted. Agarwal also highlighted the scale of job creation as Snabbit expanded its operations and strengthened its presence across markets. “FY26 was our first full year of operations. We started the year at 500 jobs a day and exited at 35,000. That's 70x growth in 12 months. Along the way, we acquired nearly a million customers, onboarded 20,000+ Experts, and built the infrastructure to create an entirely new consumer category,” he added. “We're not building a business that depends on spending more to grow more. We're building one where every additional layer of scale makes the underlying economics stronger. The losses of FY26 reflect what it took to create this category. The numbers of FY27 reflect what that investment is beginning to deliver,” he wrote in the social media post. Snabbit's total expenses rose to ₹194.76 crore in FY26 from ₹6.81 crore a year earlier, highlighting its efforts to capture market share in the instant home-help segment, where it competes with established player Urban Company. Costs relating to professionals were Snabbit’s largest expense at ₹63.07 crore, followed by marketing at ₹48.69 crore, employee expenses at ₹46.02 crore and service fulfilment expenses at ₹23.83 crore. Revenue included ₹10.82 crore from platform services and ₹1.42 crore from uniform sales. Snabbit reports revenue after deducting discounts it pays for to lower customers’ bills. Other income, mainly interest on bank deposits, contributed ₹14.77 crore, taking total income to ₹27.01 crore. Agarwal holds a Post Graduate Diploma in Management (PGDM) in Finance from Institute of Management Technology, Ghaziabad. He previously worked as a finance manager at White Owl before joining Zepto in 2022 as senior manager of finance. He was later elevated to the position of vice president and chief of staff at the quick-commerce company. In 2024, Agarwal founded Snabbit, an on-demand home services platform that provides verified and trained domestic help at customers’ doorsteps in approximately 10 minutes, with services starting at ₹99 per hour. indian-startups-07add413f3.headline: Snabbit reports Rs 12 Cr revenue and Rs 168 Cr loss in FY26; claims 75X growth in core biz
indian-startups-07add413f3.fulltext:
Two-year-old Snabbit posted a Rs 168 crore loss in FY26 on operating revenue of Rs 12.25 crore, pointing to the steep costs of building an on-demand home services business. Yet the losses are not unique to Snabbit: rivals Urban Company’s InstaHelp and Pronto are also spending heavily to scale, as players race to build demand and establish leadership.
Snabbit’s revenue from operations stood at Rs 12.25 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 26 lakh in FY25, according to its annual financial statements sourced from the Registrar of Companies (RoC).
Founded in 2024 by Aayush Agarwal, Snabbit is an on-demand home services platform that connects households with trained professionals for tasks such as cleaning, dishwashing and laundry. Users can book professionals by the hour, with the platform promising service within 10 minutes.
Platform services contributed Rs 10.82 crore, or 88% of its operating revenue, while the remaining amount came from the sale of uniforms.
The company also earned Rs 14.76 crore in other income, mainly from interest on bank deposits. Snabbit earned more from interest on its bank deposits than from its core operations. This has been common among consumer internet businesses in their early years, as they navigate intense competition and invest in growth.
On the cost side, employee benefits accounted for Rs 46 crore, while expert service costs stood at Rs 63 crore. Snabbit spent another Rs 49 crore on marketing and Rs 23.8 crore on service fulfilment. Banking charges, commissions, recruitment, legal expenses, software maintenance and other overheads pushed its total expenses to Rs 195 crore in FY26 from Rs 6.8 crore in FY25.
Heavy spending on customer acquisition, workers and service delivery pushed its net loss to Rs 168 crore in FY26 from Rs 5.7 crore in the previous fiscal year. At the unit level, Snabbit spent Rs 15.92 to earn every rupee of operating revenue.
Given how new the category is, traditional profitability metrics may not tell the entire story at this stage. However, Snabbit reported a negative return on capital employed (ROCE) of 58.45% and an EBITDA margin of -1481.63% in FY26.
Snabbit has raised over $112 million, including a$56 million Series D round from Susquehanna VC, Mirae Asset Venture Investments and Bertelsmann India Investments.
The startup has reported growing demand. It said it crossed 115,000 fulfilled jobs in a day and completed four million jobs in househelp during Q1 FY27. Burn per job declined by more than Rs 100 quarter-on-quarter to below Rs 250.
Snabbit founder Aayush Agarwal said FY26 was the company’s first full year of operations. It scaled from around 500 daily jobs across eight micro-markets at the start of the year to 35,000 daily jobs across more than 100 micro-markets by year end, a 75X increase in daily jobs. The company also acquired nearly one million customers and onboarded over 20,000 experts.
Agarwal said the Rs 167.8 crore loss reflected investments in expansion, customer and expert acquisition, and long-term capabilities. He added that “FY26 financials do not reflect current economics”, citing improvements in operating leverage and unit economics as the business built density across neighbourhoods.
Snabbit is not alone in turning household chores into a quick-commerce-style business. Urban Company’s InstaHelp completed around 1.9 million orders in July 2026, ahead of Snabbit’s 1.85 million, while Pronto crossed 1.25 million bookings.
The competition is also forcing established firm Urban Company to invest in quick home services and it has been looking to raise$200 million, while Snabbit and Pronto continue to expand.
For now, the companies are racing to win customers, build their workforce and fulfil orders faster. The key question is how long they can sustain heavy spending before the business pays for itself. Until then, the market may see more funding, higher order volumes and continued losses.
The quick home services market is entering a phase where scale alone may not translate into a durable advantage. Faster fulfilment and repeat usage can help build customer habits, but the economics will depend on whether platforms can improve worker utilisation, reduce acquisition costs and generate enough bookings within each neighbourhood to absorb fixed costs. The next test is not simply who captures demand first, but who can turn that demand into a sustainable business without relying on repeated funding rounds.

india-c3089b39a1.headline: India notifies first tariff cuts under New Zealand FTA
india-c3089b39a1.fulltext:
In a notification issued late on Friday, the Department of Revenue prescribed customs duty and cess rates for specified products, along with tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for select imports. The concessions are subject to tariff classification, product-specific conditions and proof of New Zealand origin.
Also Read: Commerce Ministry organizes “Leveraging FTAs” outreach program in Jaipur to boost exports
Specified fresh, chilled and frozen sheep meat imports will attract zero basic customs duty (BCD), agriculture infrastructure and development cess (AIDC) and health cess under the relevant tariff entries. Certain fish tariff lines will attract a 25.71% BCD, with zero AIDC and health cess. Wine imports covered by the notification will attract 20% BCD, while AIDC will vary according to the product's cost, insurance and freight (CIF) value. For a 750 ml container valued at $5 or more but below $15, the AIDC rate is 75%. For a container valued at $15 or more, it is 50%.
Specified manuka honey imports valued at $30 per kg or more will attract 51% BCD. The notification also provides an annual TRQ of 40 tonnes for qualifying honey valued at $20 per kg or more but below $30 per kg, at an in-quota BCD rate of 51%. The quota is subject to prescribed conditions, including certification requirements.
Also Read: US' Russia sanction waiver a relief for India's exporters, energy security: Experts
For specified kiwi fruit imports valued at $2.50 per kg or more, the notified BCD is 15%. An annual TRQ of 200 tonnes has also been prescribed for albumins, including milk-derived proteins, with an in-quota BCD of 10%.
Beyond food and beverages, the notification provides zero-BCD treatment for specified furniture and related products, including certain metal furniture, wooden bedroom furniture, aircraft seats and furniture parts, lamps and lighting fittings.
India has excluded several sensitive product categories, including dairy products and specified agricultural goods, from tariff liberalisation under the agreement. The TRQ provisions apply only within the prescribed quantities and are subject to the conditions in the notification. Importers must also satisfy the applicable origin requirements to claim preferential treatment, the notification said.
India's bilateral trade in goods with New Zealand stood at about $1.13 billion in 2025-26, according to the latest commerce and industry ministry data.
